tagline: Rolling hills, an early inn and a college above the village
intro: The Granville Scenic Byway runs through rural hill country in central Ohio. Ohio’s byways brochure highlights its rolling hills, farms, residential districts and Denison University. The state’s route description gives an approximately 10-mile journey beginning at State Route 37 and continuing north onto State Route 661.

Granville’s early travelers could lodge at Orrin Granger’s inn, which opened in 1812 as The Tavern and also served as a post office. It became the Buxton Inn when Major Horton Buxton bought it in 1865. Education reshaped the village too: the college founded in 1831 moved to a hill north of the village in 1855, soon after taking the name Denison University.

Begin at State Route 37, meet James Road and continue north on State Route 661. South of the village center lies Raccoon Creek’s flood plain; farther north, the village sits among three hills. Sugarloaf marks Broadway’s west end, Mt. Parnassus its east end, and College Hill rises to the north.

moments.title: Buxton Inn
moments.text: The Buxton Inn’s red exterior and white columns frame a two-story front porch. Orrin Granger opened it in 1812 as The Tavern, combining lodging with a post office. James W. Dilley bought it in 1858 and called it The Dilley House; Major Horton Buxton gave it another name after buying it in 1865. Local preservationists Orville and Audrey Orr acquired and refurbished the property in 1972. The inn joined the National Register of Historic Places in December of that year. The inn now comprises five houses, with a courtyard between the wings of the L-shaped main house.
moments.notice: White columns line both levels of the red inn’s front porch.

moments.title: Alligator Effigy Mound
moments.text: The name Alligator does not settle what this earthen figure represents. In 1999, Brad Lepper and Tod A. Frolking investigated the mound and dated charcoal from its base, estimating construction at about AD 950. Lepper suggests that the figure represents an underwater panther from Native American myth. He thinks early European settlers misunderstood a description of a fierce water creature and assumed it meant an alligator. The mound occupies privately owned land accessible to the public, and an Ohio historical marker identifies the site. It is one of two surviving effigy mounds known in Ohio, along with Serpent Mound.

moments.title: Swasey Chapel
moments.text: Swasey Chapel was the first building in Denison’s Greater Denison campus plan. Completed in 1924, it honors Ambrose Swasey, a Cleveland inventor, businessman and college benefactor. The chapel stands at the campus center and seats 990. Its uses extend beyond religious services to lectures, concerts and academic award convocations.
